description:
## Uncertainty Quantification of Gap-Induced Manufacturing Defects in Open-Hole Tension

### Introduction

Manufacturing defects are an unavoidable consequence of composite fabrication processes and can significantly influence the structural integrity of aerospace components. Among these defects, gaps generated during Automated Fibre Placement (AFP) may locally alter the stiffness and stress distribution, potentially reducing the notched strength of structural laminates. Quantifying the influence of these geometric imperfections requires large ensembles of high-fidelity finite element (FE) simulations, making High-Performance Computing (HPC) an essential enabler for Uncertainty Quantification (UQ) analysis. This workflow corresponds to one of the case studies presented by [S. Abdel-Monsef et al. 2026](add_doi).

### Workflow and Use-Case

This example employs the `MONTECARLO` workflow available in the [CAELESTIS Workflows](https://github.com/CAELESTIS-Project-EU/Workflows) to perform large-scale UQ through Monte Carlo sampling. The workflow combines [PyCOMPSs](https://doi.org/10.14279/depositonce-25823) as the task-based workflow manager and HPC orchestrator with [Alya](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jocs.2015.12.007) as the high-performance finite element (FE) solver responsible for generating high-fidelity synthetic data. An overview of the workflow is presented in **Figure 1**.

![Figure 1](https://workflowhub.eu/workflows/2242/git/1/raw/dataset/img/Fig_Monte_Carlo_HPC_workflow.svg)

**Figure 1.** *HPC-based Monte Carlo workflow for high-fidelity synthetic data generation of coupons. PyCOMPSs orchestrates the distributed execution of the workflow, while Alya performs the finite element simulations that generate the synthetic data.*

The workflow consists of four main stages:

  1. **Sampling:** A design of experiments (DoE) based on Latin Hypercube Sampling (LHS), implemented using the [PyDOE](https://pydoe.github.io/pydoe/) package, generates samples from the prescribed probability distributions.
  2. **FE model generation:** [COUPONtool](https://github.com/CAELESTIS-Project-EU/COUPONtool) automatically generates high-fidelity FE model in [Alya](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jocs.2015.12.007) for each sample.
  3. **Simulation:** [Alya](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jocs.2015.12.007) solves in parallel the structural mechanics problem with progressive damage for each realization.
  4. **Post-processing:** The simulation outputs are automatically collected and aggregated into a synthetic dataset for statistical analysis and uncertainty quantification.

  This workflow reproduces 128 samples from the study of gap-induced manufacturing defects presented in [S. Abdel-Monsef et al. 2026](add_doi). The use-case consists of an Open-Hole Tension (OHT) laminate with stacking sequence `[-45/0/45/90]_3S`, manufactured from the IMS65/RTM6 material system using unidirectional tapes from [TeXtreme](https://textreme.com). The specimen dimensions are 36 mm in width (`W`), 54 mm in length (`L`), with a 6 mm diameter (`D`) central hole. An in-plane element size of 0.366 mm is used, resulting in meshes compromising approximately 680,000 elements. The parameterized high-fidelity FE model is illustrated in **Figure 2**.

  ![Figure 2](https://workflowhub.eu/workflows/2242/git/1/raw/dataset/img/Fig_Monte_Carlo_Alya_FEM_OHT_gaps.svg)

  **Figure 2.** *Parametric high-fidelity finite element model of the Open-Hole Tension specimen containing AFP-induced two-gap manufacturing defects.*

  The study investigates the isolated influence of Automated Fiber Placement (AFP) with two-gap manufacturing defects while keeping all material properties deterministic. Three geometrical parameters are treated as random variables for the two-gaps:

  - Gap width, `G_W` ~ U(4.5, 5.5) mm
  - Gap distance from the hole center, `D_c` ~ U(-1.5, 3.5) mm
  - Gap ply location, `Ply_i` ~ U(2, 23)

  This example reproduces 128 high-fidelity Monte Carlo simulations under tensile loading. Larger campaigns involving thousands of simulations can also be performed using the same workflow, as demonstrated by [S. Abdel-Monsef et al. 2026](add_doi). Each simulation corresponds to an independent realization of the random input parameters. Each simulation is automatically terminated once the applied load decreases by 30% from its peak value. This HPC workflow dramatically reduces the overall time-to-solution and provides an efficient, scalable, and fully reproducible framework for high-fidelity synthetic data generation and uncertainty quantification.

### Results and Conclusions

A success rate of 100% is achieved across the 128 high-fidelity simulations, demonstrating the robustness of the Alya FE solver and the proposed HPC workflow. The Monte Carlo simulations predict tensile strengths in the range of 458.1 - 469.0 MPa with a mean value of 463.5 MPa. **Figure 3** depicts the histogram, empirical cumulative distribution function (ECDF), and bootstrap-based KDE of the 10th percentile from the DoE investigated.

![Figure 3](https://workflowhub.eu/workflows/2242/git/1/raw/dataset/img/Fig_OH_Monte_Carlo_stat_128samples.svg)

**Figure 3.** *Results obtained from the 128 high-fidelity simulations of the Open-Hole Tension specimen with AFP two-gap induced manufacturing defects.*

These results ivestigate the localized influence of manufacturing gaps on the tensile strength. The reader is referred to [S. Abdel-Monsef et al. 2026](add_doi) for the larger simulation campaigns and case studies on the uncertainties arising from material properties, geometry and their combined effects. Overall, the proposed HPC framework enables efficient propagation of manufacturing uncertainties through high-fidelity composite simulations and can be readily extended to other defect types, material uncertainties, and structural configurations.

### Prerequisites

 - Access to the MareNostrum5 supercomputer or an equivalent HPC system.
 - Access to a compiled version of Alya distributed under a Limited Use License (LUL)

As the required software and execution environment are not publicly distributed, please contact the workflow author for information on reproducing or replicating this workflow.

### Reproducibility

1. Download this package and copy it to your working directory on MareNostrum5.
2. Navigate to the application directory:
   ```bash
   cd application_sources
   ```
3. Edit the `run_from_crate.sh` script and update the `PROJECT_NAME` and `QOS` variables according to your allocation.
   By default each simulation uses 112 CPU cores, and the workflow allocates 32 nodes from MareNostrum5 (3,584 CPU cores in total) to execute the Monte Carlo simulations concurrently.
4. Submit the workflow using:
   ```bash
   bash run_from_crate.sh
   ```
   A folder named as `SIMULATIONS` will be created containing all the samples.
5. To monitor the results by plotting the force-displacement curves:
   ```python 
   python plot_all_f-d.py
   ```
6. Once the workflow has completed, execute the post-processing scripts to collect the simulation results and generate the statistical analysis:
   ```python 
   python post_collect.py
   python plot_statistics.py ./results/montecarlo_oht_only_gaps_res.npz
   ```
   The `plot_all_f-d.py` script plots all the resulting force-displacement curves while the `plot_statistics.py` script generates the histogram, empirical cumulative distribution function (ECDF), bootstrap-based KDE of the 10th percentile, and the corresponding statistical summary of the predicted open-hole tensile strength distribution due to the presence of two manufacturing gaps.

> :warning: The execution of this DoE requires a total disk space of approximately 32 GB and takes a wall-clock time of approximately 1 h and 35 min. The execution of larger campaings such as, 1,000 simulations with 125 nodes of MareNostrum5 requires a total disk space of approximatedly 280 GB and takes a wall-clock time of less than 4 hours.

### Replicability: Running the workflow with a different configuration

To execute the workflow using a different configuration (e.g., a different number of samples, probability distributions, or CPU cores per simulation), perform the following steps:

1. Navigate to the input configuration directory:
   ```bash
   cd dataset/inputs
   ```
2. Open the `montecarlo_oht_only_gaps.yaml` file and modify the following parameters:
   ```yaml
    - seed: 123
    - n_samples: 128   # Default
    - ALYA_PROCS: 112  # Default
    ```
   where:
    - `seed` specifies the random seed used for sampling, to disable it, set it to `null`.
    - `n_samples` specifies the number of Monte Carlo simulations.
    - `ALYA_PROCS` specifies the number of CPU cores assigned to each Alya simulation.

Modifying any other field requires advanced knowledge of the workflow configuration and is recommended only for experienced users.

### Publication

If you use this workflow in your work, please cite this repository and the following publication. Sharing advances science.

S. Abdel-Monsef, G. Guillamet, J. Ejarque, R. Cecco, A. Turon, R. M. Badia,
*Uncertainty Quantification of Defects in Composite Structures Using High-Fidelity Simulations and HPC Resources*,
(under publication)
